title: Mishpatim: the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:21–23)
hookLine: God hears the cry of the widow and the fatherless
tomorrow: Mishpatim: we will do, and we will hear (Exodus 24:7)

lines: THE ONE NOBODY STANDS UP FOR.
cards: In an office there can be someone no one stands up for: the temp, the new hire with no friends yet, the cleaner who comes in after everyone's gone. If someone takes advantage of them, who will complain?
Who will even notice? In the ancient world, the people in that position had names. A widow, with no husband to speak for her in court.
An orphan, with no father to protect his inheritance. Easy people to cheat. The Torah turns to them directly, and does something unusual: it names who is listening.

teach.h: YE SHALL NOT AFFLICT ANY WIDOW.
teach.b: Here's the law, in the old Jewish translation: "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child."

teach.h: DOUBLED VERBS: SURELY I WILL HEAR.
teach.b: Then: if you afflict them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry. In Hebrew, three verbs in that line are doubled. Afflict, you afflict.
Cry, they cry. Hear, I will hear. It's the Hebrew way of saying: really, surely, I mean it.
The next verse is fierce. It warns that the one who harms them will meet the same fate, their own wives widowed, their own children fatherless. Measure for measure.
The Torah doesn't soften it, and this lesson won't either.

teach.h: RASHI: EVERYONE, BUT THE WEAKEST FIRST.
teach.b: Rashi asks a fair question. Is it only widows and orphans you mustn't afflict? No, he says, following the Mekhilta: the same law covers every person.
The Torah names these two because they're the weakest and the easiest to hurt. The law speaks where the danger is greatest.
Who has no protection now? A tenant without a lease. An elderly person living alone.
A child in foster care. A worker far from home. The categories change; the shape doesn't.

And notice where the verse puts God: not on the side of the powerful, the judge or the landowner, but at the ear of the person crying. Isaiah picks this up, telling Israel to judge the fatherless and plead for the widow.

how: Jewish communities have kept funds and societies for widows, orphans and the poor, and Jewish law, following Rashi and the Mekhilta, applies the ban on afflicting the widow and orphan to every person, with special care for the vulnerable.

o: the law of freeing servants after six years
ordinances: the rules a court would use
a widow's plea brought before the judges

games.q: inside the law — tap the pairs.
p: no husband to speak for her in court
no father to guard his inheritance

s: Rashi says it's fine to afflict people who aren't widows or orphans
he says the law covers everyone; these two are named because they're weakest.
the Hebrew doubles the verbs: afflict, cry, hear
the doubling is a way of saying surely.
the Torah softens its warning in the next verse
it's fierce: measure for measure, the harm comes back on the one who did it.

games.q: the law names the widow and the orphan. you're Rashi. does that mean everyone else is fair game?
o: yes, only these two are protected.
no, it covers everyone; the weakest are named first.
games.why: every person. the Torah speaks where the danger is greatest: the people easiest to hurt.

practice: Let one person around you who has nobody to speak for them come into focus: an older neighbor living alone, a new coworker, a kid at the edge of the playground. What do they need that they can't ask for?
If you pray, you can hold them before God, who the verse says surely hears; if not, simply listen, the way you'd want someone to listen to you.

wordCard.voice: Mishpatim. The ordinances. Today, the law that protects the widow and the fatherless, and says God surely hears their cry.

orig.note: Hebrew: orphan, the fatherless child named beside the widow in Exodus 22:21.

carryVoice: Your line: God hears them. The quietest cry is the one the verse names. See you tomorrow.
